description: We represent the American Institute of Chemical Engineering KBTU Chapter. We are a team of students who want to contribute to space exploration development using our chemistry, biology and other technical skills.
summary:
Even on the station, medical care, supplies and instructions are harder
to get than on Earth, distance from Earth makes medical care harder, so health must be assessed on board. AIChE Health is a native software program for Linux and Windows that monitors the health of the crew of a space station or spacecraft without any connection to Earth. It works completely locally: without a browser, clouds, and the internet. Earth norms give false alarms, but the real danger can be missed. Therefore, four levels are set for each analysis: the norm on Earth, the norm in space, unsettling, dangerous. Portable sensors transmit data on the frequency of heart contractions and respiration to onboard computing devices, AI models at the border perform analysis of anomalies in real time, and only if problems are detected is an alarm or a decision to return initiated, without the need to wait for analysis from the ground center. NASA is already moving towards real-time diagnostics (T empus Pro, CANS), which fits our software in that direction.
details:
1. Introduction

AIChE Health is a native Linux and Windows program that monitors the health of a space station or spacecraft crew without any contact with Earth. It runs entirely locally: no browser, cloud, or internet.

In space body changes fast, meanwhile doctors are on Earth.

Spaceflight changes the body every day: bone, blood, fluids, eyes, sleep and mood. Three figures show the scale:

  • 1–1.5% of bone mass is lost every month without gravity.
  • 54% more red blood cells are destroyed over the whole stay in microgravity.
  • About 2 liters of fluid shift toward the chest and head, loading the eyes and neck veins.

NASA names five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile, closed environments. The team focuses on distance from Earth, because medical care, supplies and instructions are hardest to get there.

There is a second problem. Most crew samples are frozen and analyzed on Earth after the crew returns, so the crew gets no live feedback. Earth reference ranges also misfire on board. In the demo mission, 47 of 73 values look abnormal by Earth norms yet are normal in space. Earth ranges therefore raise false alarms and can miss real danger, which is why monitoring has to run on board, 24/7.

Therefore, our program aims to solve these problems via novel solutions.

The program has two parts:

- aiche-core is the “brain”. It stores data in SQLite, evaluates lab results against space-specific thresholds, calculates the health index, and runs the offline advisor. It is accessible only on this computer (address 127.0.0.1).

- aiche-health is the window with the interface (eight sections). By default it runs the core inside itself, so a single file is enough.

Data is stored in profiles, which are ordinary JSON files containing the mission, the crew roster, and all their data (lab results, questionnaires, pain, MoCA). On first launch the program is empty, with no fictional data: you create a mission and add crew, or load a ready-made profile.

Main idea: Earth norms give false alarms and can miss real danger. For this reason, every lab test has four levels: Earth normal, space normal, concerning, and dangerous.

for example: internal jugular vein area:

  • Earth normal: 0.4–1.0 cm²
  • Space normal: 1.5–2.5 cm²
  • Concerning: 2.6–3.5 cm²
  • Dangerous: above 3.5 cm²

The program combines three things:

  • 73 biomarkers, each read on a space-specific scale.
  • 7 body systems, rolled into one health index from 0 to 100.
  • 14 clinical rules in an advisor that explains every alert.

The seven systems are:

  • Cardio & Blood (19 markers): neck-vein ultrasound, ECG, hemoglobin, clotting.
  • Musculoskeletal (13): bone turnover, calcium, muscle ultrasound.
  • Neuro-sensory (11): eye scans for SANS, sleep EEG, brain pressure.
  • Metabolic & Renal (18): kidney-stone profile, liver, glucose, gut.
  • Immune & Endocrine (12): cortisol, T-cells, latent viruses, radiation dose.
  • Mind: daily check-in, reaction test, weekly MoCA, entered by the crew.
  • Pain: body map with zone, intensity, type and duration, entered by the crew.

How it works?

  1. Record. The crew logs lab and ultrasound results, a daily mental check-in, a reaction test, pain on a body map and a mandatory weekly MoCA.
  2. Score. Each value lands on its space-specific scale: normal, concerning or dangerous.
  3. Index. Seven system scores form a 0–100 health index and a status: NOMINAL, WATCH or CRITICAL.
  4. Advise. Rules combine markers, mind and pain into alerts with evidence and a checklist of actions.

2. Launching

Windows

Needs Visual Studio 2022+ with the workload "Desktop development with C++" (it includes the compiler and CMake). The script finds CMake even if it is not on PATH ("cmake is not recognized"):

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build_windows.ps1 -Run

Without -Run it only builds; start the app with cd build; .\ui\Release\aiche-health.exe. If you prefer the commands by hand, run them in "Developer PowerShell for VS" (Start menu), where cmake is available: cmake -S . -B build; cmake --build build --config Release.

Linux (Ubuntu / Debian)

./scripts/build_linux.sh

cd build && ./ui/aiche-health

Or with Docker (headless core smoke test): docker build -t aiche-health . && docker run --rm aiche-health.

macOS (not yet verified on real hardware)

chmod +x scripts/build_macos.sh && ./scripts/build_macos.sh

Needs Xcode Command Line Tools and CMake (the script installs CMake via Homebrew if present). Uses the system OpenGL 3.2 core profile (deprecated by Apple but still available).

Options

aiche-health [--profile FILE] [--profiles DIR] [--connect] [--port N] [--size WxH] [--shot DIR]

  • default: runs the core inside the UI process (still over local HTTP)
  • --connect: attach to a separately running aiche-core --data data --profiles profiles
  • --shot DIR: render each screen to PNG (used for documentation)

Data

data/biomarkers.json is generated from the protocol spreadsheet: python tools/xlsx_to_json.py data/source/Spaceflight_Diagnostic_Biomarker_Values.xlsx data/biomarkers.json

3. Window overview

Fig. 1. The “Crew Overview” screen. Menu and crew on the left, mission status bar on top.

Top Bar

  • MISSION DAY 74 / 180: current mission day and progress.
  • COMMS: OFFLINE: a reminder that there is no contact with Earth and the system operates autonomously.
  • REFERENCE: SPACE / EARTH NORMS: reference switch. In Earth mode, the lab screen highlights values that look abnormal by Earth norms but are normal in space.
  • SIM +1 DAY / NEXT DAY: advances to the next mission day. In a simulated (demo) mission, fictional measurements, questionnaires, and events appear; in a regular mission the button only advances the day counter.

Left Menu

  • Eight sections: Crew Overview, Vitals & Labs, Mind, MoCA Test, Body Map, Advisor, Mission Report, and (separately at the bottom) Mission & Crew.
  • Colored badges: next to Advisor, the number of active alerts; next to Vitals & Labs, the number of out-of-range indicators; next to MoCA Test, the number of crew members with an overdue test.
  • At the bottom is the crew list. The ring around the avatar shows status: green is normal, yellow is watch, red is critical. Clicking a person switches all screens to them.

Statuses

Status When assigned

NOMINAL(green) No out-of-range values, feeling fine

WATCH(yellow) There are concerning values, or the Mind score is below 55, or pain is 6/10 or higher, or the weekly MoCA is overdue

CRITICAL(red) There is a dangerous lab value, or pain is 8/10 or higher, or the Mind score is below 30

4. Main Functions by Screen

4.1 Crew Overview

The first screen for the commander and medical officer: who is fine and who needs help right now.

  • Red banner appears if anyone has critical status. Clicking it opens the advisor for that person.
  • Yellow “Weekly MoCA due” banner lists those who are due (or overdue) for weekly testing. Clicking it opens the MoCA screen.
  • Crew cards: the ring is the health index 0–100; below it are alert statistics and MoCA status; below that are seven bars representing body systems (hover to see the name and score). Clicking a card selects the person. If there is no data yet, a NO DATA YET label is shown.
  • System Balance: a radar of seven systems: blood and heart, muscles and bones, nervous system and vision, metabolism and kidneys, immunity and hormones, mind, pain. The closer to the edge, the better.
  • Priority Alerts: the main warnings for the selected person and a list of out-of-range indicators.

Mission Log: an event journal: an indicator became concerning, pain was reported, etc. Stored locally until a communication session.

4.2 Vitals & Labs

Fig. 2. The “Vitals & Labs” screen: test list, threshold scale, and details panel.

This screen has 73 indicators across five body systems. For each, the device and measurement frequency are shown.

  • Filters at the top: all systems or one of the five; the “Onboard-capable only” button leaves only tests that can be done on board.
  • Test row: name, device, availability tag (ONBOARD: device is on board; LIMITED: with limitations; NEEDS KIT: additional kit required), value, scale, mini-graph, and status.
  • Scale: the green zone is normal in space, yellow is concerning, red is dangerous. The white line with a circle is the current value.
  • Right panel (click a row): history graph over the zones, text of all four levels, device, and frequency.
  • Entering a new measurement: enter a number and press RECORD. The program immediately reports how it evaluated the value and updates the index, advisor, and log.
  • In Earth norms mode, rows that are normal for space but outside the Earth norm get an EARTH FLAG label

4.3 Mind: Mental Health

Fig. 3. The “Mind” screen: daily questionnaire, reaction test, and graphs.

Three blocks from left to right:

  • Daily Mental Check-in: six sliders from 1 to 10: mood, stress, anxiety, fatigue, isolation and confinement, sleep quality. The color of the value shows whether it is good or bad. Press SUBMIT CHECK-IN. Data stays on this computer.
  • Reaction Test (PVT): a psychomotor vigilance test. Click the circle (START), wait, and click again as soon as the circle turns green. There are 5 trials in total. If you click too early, the trial counts as an error and you must start over. Average time: up to 280 ms is good, up to 350 ms is concerning, above that is dangerous. The SAVE RESULT button saves the result together with the current questionnaire.
  • Trends: a 30-day graph. The Mood, Stress, Anxiety, Fatigue, and Isolation buttons toggle the lines. Below are bars of reaction time for the most recent measurements.

The advisor uses this data: rising stress, anxiety, low mood, or isolation trigger a recommendation for psychological support.

4.4 MoCA Test: Weekly Cognitive Check

Fig. 4. The “MoCA Test” screen: status and graph on the left, new assessment form on the right.

The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is a 30-point screening of cognitive function. Every crew member is required to take it once every 7 days. The program tracks the schedule and won’t let you forget it:

  • If 7 or more days have passed since the last test, yellow banners appear on the MoCA screen and the overview, the person’s status is at least WATCH, and the advisor creates a “Weekly MoCA overdue” alert. After 14 days the alert becomes critical. A new person with no records immediately gets a requirement to take a baseline test.
  • The person takes the test, and the test administrator enters the scores in the form on the right. The program does not show the tasks itself: use the official licensed MoCA materials (mocacognition.com).
  • The form: test version (8.1, 8.2, 8.3; the program suggests the next one in rotation to reduce the practice effect), time in minutes, and seven domains: visuospatial and executive functions (max 5), naming (3), attention (6), language (3), abstraction (2), delayed recall (5), orientation (6).
  • The total is calculated automatically. If education is 12 years or less, +1 point is added (the education field is set in the person’s card). A score of 26 or higher is normal; 18–25 is mild impairment; 10–17 is moderate; below 10 is severe.
  • On the left: a ring with the latest result, the due date for the next test, the version for next time, and a graph of the last 12 tests with a normal line at 26.
  • The advisor additionally reacts to a result below 26 and to a drop of 3 points or more from the person’s personal baseline. MoCA contributes 30% to the Mind system score.

The test does not block other functions: you can always report pain or enter a lab result, even with an overdue MoCA.

4.5 Body Map: Pain Map

Fig. 5. The “Body Map” screen: figure from front and back, form and active pain reports on the right.

If an astronaut feels pain, they show the location on the figure:

  • Hover over the body: a zone is highlighted (head, neck, chest, lower back, knee, etc.). The figure matches the selected person’s sex.
  • Click the desired spot on the front or back view. A crosshair appears and a form opens on the right.
  • Set the intensity 1–10, pain type (dull, sharp, burning, throbbing, pressing, numbness), duration in hours, and a note.
  • Press SUBMIT PAIN REPORT. A pulsing marker appears on the body: green (1–3), yellow (4–6), red (7–10).
  • In the Active Reports list, the Resolved button closes the complaint when the pain has gone.
  • Pain of 7/10 or higher immediately creates a critical alert. Pain is also factored into the rules (for example, neck pain when venous thrombosis is suspected).

4.6 Advisor: Autonomous Advisor

Fig. 6. The “Advisor” screen: alert, evidence, and action list.

The advisor works on board without the internet. It combines labs, mental state, and pain using 14 rules and produces cards sorted by importance:

  • Title and level (CRITICAL / WATCH) and the affected system.
  • Evidence: which specific indicators and reports triggered the rule, so the logic can be checked.
  • Recommended Actions: concrete steps. Tick the checkboxes as you complete them (ticks are saved while the program is open).

Examples of rules: spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS), accelerated bone loss, kidney stone risk, muscle damage, cardiac rhythm disturbances, jugular vein thrombosis, space anemia, fatigue and circadian rhythm disruption, chronic stress and immunity, radiation, metabolism, lower back and spine, psychological strain, severe pain.

4.7 Mission Report: Report for Earth

Fig. 7. The “Mission Report” screen: report text and send queue.

The report briefly describes the person’s condition: index, system scores, out-of-range indicators, active pains, and advisor conclusions.

  • Export this crew member: saves the selected person’s report to the file report_Name_dayN.txt in the folder from which the program was launched.
  • Export all crew: reports for everyone.
  • Copy to clipboard: copies the text to the clipboard.
  • Downlink Queue: a list of prepared files waiting for a communication session. Actual sending is not implemented: files must be transferred manually.

4.8 Mission & Crew: Profiles, Mission, and Crew Roster

Fig. 8. The “Mission & Crew” screen: profiles, mission parameters, and crew editor.

Everything that was previously “hard-coded” into the program is configured here. Three columns:

  • Mission Profiles: a list of JSON profiles from the profiles folder. The LOAD button loads a profile (changing the flight, station, or roster). NEW BLANK MISSION creates an empty mission (name, vehicle/station, flight type, duration). Save copy as saves a copy under a different name.
  • Mission: name, station or vehicle, flight type (station, spacecraft, lunar base, Mars transit, Mars base), duration, current day. The “Simulated mission” checkbox enables the demo data generator for the SIM +1 DAY button. Press APPLY MISSION CHANGES.
  • Crew: the + ADD MEMBER button adds a person. Select a person in the list and change their name, role (can be taken from templates), sex (reference values depend on it), age, height, weight, education in years, medical notes, and allergies. SAVE CHANGES saves; DELETE removes the person along with all their data (requires a second click to confirm).

All changes are saved to the profile file automatically; there is no separate “Save” item.

Profile Format

A profile is plain-text JSON; it can be edited manually or prepared in another system. An example is profiles/template_empty_mission.json. Structure:

{ "format": "aiche-health-profile", "version": 1,

"mission": { name, vehicle, type, duration_days, day, simulated },

"crew": [ { id, name, role, sex ("M"|"F"), age, height_cm, weight_kg, education_years,

notes,

"data": { labs: [{bio, day, value}], mind: [...], pain: [...], moca: [...] } } ],

"events": [ ... ] }

Lab identifiers (the bio field) come from the file data/biomarkers.json. Unknown identifiers are skipped on load.

5. Typical Scenarios

Scenario 0. New mission from scratch

  • Mission & Crew → NEW BLANK MISSION → name, station/vehicle, duration → CREATE.
    • ADD MEMBER for each crew member, fill in the data, and press SAVE CHANGES.
  • Immediately take a baseline MoCA for each person and enter lab results on the Vitals and Mind screens.

Scenario 1. Quick morning overview

  • Open Crew Overview. If there is a red banner, click it.
  • In Advisor, read the evidence and carry out the actions, ticking the checkboxes.
  • Export the report in Mission Report.

Scenario 2. New lab result

  • Vitals & Labs → find the indicator (by system or in the list) → enter the value → RECORD.
  • Look at the evaluation in the notification at the bottom of the screen and the change in the health index.

Scenario 3. An astronaut reports pain

  • Select the person in the list on the left → Body Map → click the pain location → intensity and type → SUBMIT PAIN REPORT.
  • Open Advisor: the pain may have strengthened a related alert.

Scenario 3b. Weekly MoCA

  • MoCA Test → select the person → enter scores for the seven domains → SAVE ASSESSMENT. The overdue banner will disappear.

Scenario 4. Mental check

  • Select the person → Mind → fill in the questionnaire → SUBMIT CHECK-IN.
  • Take the Reaction Test (5 trials) and save the result.

Scenario 5. Jury demonstration (about 2 minutes)

  • Overview: red banner, Marcus Okafor in critical condition. Show the crew index rings.
  • Advisor: probable jugular vein thrombosis, evidence (ultrasound, D-dimer, neck pain) and actions.
  • Labs: switch on Earth norms and show how many false alarms Earth norms produce. Open one indicator and show the zones and history.
  • Body Map: mark chest pain 8/10, return to the overview and show the new alert.
  • MoCA: show the overdue warning for Arjun Mehta and enter a result. Mind: take the reaction test. Press SIM +1 DAY and show the events in the log. Export the report.
  • Mission & Crew: load a different profile or add a new crew member to show the system’s flexibility.

Demo Profile (demo_expedition.json)

Crew member Role Scenario

Elena Vasquez Commander Neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS), rising stress, declining MoCA

Arjun Mehta Flight engineer Bone loss, kidney stone risk, lower back pain, overdue MoCA

Yuki Tanaka Mission specialist Everything normal (control case)

Marcus Okafor Medical Officer Probable jugular vein thrombosis (critical)

6. Questions and Answers

Q1: Is the internet needed?

A1: No everything works locally. The API address is 127.0.0.1 only

Q2: Where is the data stored?

A2: In the profile’s JSON file in the profiles folder. It is updated automatically after every change. Copy the file to make a backup.

Q3: How do I start with a clean slate?

A3: Mission & Crew → NEW BLANK MISSION. Demo data is loaded only if you load the demo profile yourself.

Q4: Do I need to take MoCA if everything is fine?

A4: Yes, once every 7 days for each crew member. The program will remind you and flag overdue tests.

Q5: The window is empty or says “No data”

A5: The core is unavailable (if you launched with --connect, start aiche-core first), or the profile has no crew members; add them in Mission & Crew.

Q6: Port 8787 is busy

A6: Specify another: --port 8800 (and the same value for aiche-core and the window).

Q7: How do I switch people?

A7: Click a name in the list on the left (bottom of the menu) or a card on the overview.

Q8: Is the data real?

A8: Not in the demo profile: the crew and measurements are fictional. You fill your own profiles with real data yourself; remember this is a prototype, not a medical device.

Energy

Crew data stays on board in local files (mission profiles). Compact reports wait in a downlink queue until the next link to Earth, so data never leaves the vehicle unless the crew exports a report.

The measured footprint of the core is:

  • About 9 MB of memory in use.
  • 2.5 MB executable size.
  • About 2 ms to return the full crew state.
  • About 0% CPU while idle.

The core is a rule engine instead of a neural network. It computes only when a value is recorded and needs no GPU, so its energy cost is close to the idle cost of the computer it runs on. It is written in C++17 with every dependency vendored, needs no cloud or internet at runtime, and can run headless while several displays attach.

The measurements come from a Linux x86-64 test build with a 4-person demo mission. Watts on flight hardware are not yet measured, and the slide says so openly.

7. Future

1. We aim to implement an AiChe Health AI - a specialist on board.

The roadmap has three stages:

  • Now (working prototype): 73 biomarkers on space-specific scales, an offline advisor with 14 clinical rules, and store-and-forward mission reports.
  • Next (flight-ready): thresholds validated with flight surgeons, direct links to onboard analyzers and ultrasound, and a multilingual interface with signed storage.
  • Vision (AIChE Health AI): a specialized medical model that runs on board, offline. It would predict trends before a threshold is crossed and give specialist-level analysis when no specialist is reachable. The rule engine stays as the explainable safety net.

2. Extend AIChE Health beyond the station to the Moon, Mars and other cosmic bodies

AIChE Health today is a working prototype. It monitors crew health offline on a station or spacecraft by evaluating 73 biomarkers, mental state and pain on space-specific scales. Our next goal is to adapt it for missions to the Moon, Mars and other cosmic bodies, and to build it on fault-tolerant operating systems

Today the app is a working native prototype that monitors crew health offline by evaluating 73 biomarkers, mental state and pain on space-specific scales. The next stage is to adapt it for lunar bases, Mars transit and Mars bases. The mission model is already prepared for this, because Mission & Crew supports flight types such as lunar base, Mars transit and Mars base. The crew, profile and advisor logic can therefore be reused once the ranges are adapted.

3. Build on fault-tolerant operating systems

A health monitor is only useful if it works when it is needed. A software or hardware fault far from Earth cannot be fixed by contacting engineers, so the platform itself must isolate failures and recover without stopping the whole system. Our architecture suits such a port:

  • The core is a lightweight rule engine with about 9 MB of memory in use and a 2.5 MB executable.
  • It is written in C++17 with every dependency vendored.
  • It needs no cloud, no internet and no GPU at runtime.
  • The core and the interface are separate processes, so the core can run headless while several displays attach.

Claude AI was used primarily for research as well as for the development of the code used for this project.
